text: Back in Lesson 10, we introduced sys_dictionary as the table holding one record per field, across every table in the whole instance. This lesson goes one level deeper, because that record isn't documentation sitting off to the side describing a field somewhere else. It IS the field. There is no hidden schema file the platform secretly consults instead — if you want to know what a field really is, sys_dictionary is the only place that answer lives.

Open any dictionary entry and you'll find a specific, bounded set of attributes. There's the table it belongs to, the real database column name, the label shown to users on a form, the type — string, reference, choice, and so on, which Lesson 16 covers field by field — the maximum length the database will accept, an optional default value for new records, and a set of behavior flags: Mandatory, Read-only, Active, and Unique. Every single one of those is a column on the sys_dictionary record itself, meaning you're editing real, queryable data, not configuration locked away in a file.

Here's the part that makes ServiceNow genuinely different from a hand-coded application. Check the Mandatory box on a dictionary entry and click Save, and every form built against that table — Agent Workspace, the classic UI, even forms built after today — immediately requires that field before a record can save. No developer wrote a validation rule. Nothing was deployed. The platform reads sys_dictionary live, on every single render, and that one flag is what produces the asterisk, the red border, and the save block, everywhere, instantly. That's what metadata-driven actually means in practice.

You can reach that same record two different ways. The direct path is System Definition, then Dictionary, which opens every dictionary entry in the instance as an ordinary filterable list — perfect when you're auditing a whole table at once. The faster, contextual path is right-clicking a field's label on an open form and choosing Personalize Dictionary, which jumps straight to that one field's entry without any searching at all. Learn both; you'll reach for each one in different moments.

Hold onto this idea, because the rest of the chapter builds directly on it. Field type is a dictionary attribute. A choice list is extra data tied to a dictionary entry whose type happens to be Choice. The lab coming up is really just you, by hand, filling in a brand-new dictionary entry's attributes from scratch. Next up: the common field types you'll actually be choosing between.
